images.title: Havana harbor in 1898
images.description: Yellow papers and a battleship at the bottom of Havana harbor: the war lasted one summer.

images.title: Portrait of Senator Albert Beveridge
images.description: Beveridge answered Turner: open a new frontier overseas, recapture the pioneer spirit.

images.title: The American flag in the 1890s
images.description: Deeper than greed: identity. If the frontier made us, who are we now?

images.title: An American battleship of the 1890s
images.description: What did battleships have to do with selling surplus? Mahan's answer: great powers need great navies.

images.title: Portrait of Captain Alfred Thayer Mahan
images.description: Mahan, 1890: The Influence of Sea Power upon History. Great powers need great navies; navies need coaling stations.

images.title: The title page of Mahan's Sea Power, 1890
images.description: Naval officers worldwide studied him; Roosevelt devoured him. Mahan turned sea power into national destiny.

images.title: A steamship crossing the ocean in the 1890s
images.description: Crossing an ocean on coal and faith: the world the new navy would patrol.

images.title: Portrait of Josiah Strong
images.description: Josiah Strong, 1885: God made the Anglo-Saxons their 'brother's keepers,' theology for empire.

images.title: American missionaries abroad in the 1890s
images.description: The missionaries saw empire as a chance to convert the world, blessing the whole project.

images.title: Portrait of Rudyard Kipling
images.description: Kipling's 1899 poem urging America to take up the 'White Man's Burden.'

images.title: Loading cargo in the 1890s
images.description: The whole stack: markets hungry for customers and a navy hungry for bases, with the missionaries blessing it.

images.title: An American factory in 1893
images.description: The panic, Mahan's doctrine, the missionaries, Beveridge's new frontier: the exam grades them together.

images.title: Portrait of Queen Liliuokalani of Hawaii
images.description: Hawaii was the rehearsal: American sugar planters overthrew the queen in 1893 and asked Washington to annex them.

images.title: A Hawaiian sugar plantation in the 1890s
images.description: American planters took over the economy; Cleveland refused annexation, McKinley agreed, Congress annexed Hawaii in 1898.

images.title: Pearl Harbor in the late 1800s
images.description: Pearl Harbor in the bargain: the Pacific naval base Mahan's doctrine demanded.

images.title: Cuban rebels in 1895
images.description: Cuba, ninety miles off Florida: falling sugar prices triggered a revolt against Spain in 1895.

images.title: Cuban refugees during the war
images.description: Two hundred and twenty-five thousand dead. Not a war. A catastrophe.

images.title: Portrait of Joseph Pulitzer
images.description: Pulitzer's World competed with Hearst's Journal in sensationalism: yellow journalism.

images.title: Portrait of William Randolph Hearst
images.description: Hearst's Journal: news designed to sell papers first and be true second.

images.title: The Yellow Kid comic strip
images.description: The Yellow Kid, a kid in a yellow nightshirt: the wildly popular cartoon that named yellow journalism.

images.title: The Yellow Kid in Hogan's Alley
images.description: Hearst poached Pulitzer's artist; Pulitzer hired a replacement. Two yellow kids, two rival papers, and the name stuck.

images.title: A yellow-press front page from 1898
images.description: They pushed the public, though McKinley didn't want war; he'd fought in the Civil War and knew the cost.

images.title: President William McKinley in 1898
images.description: A Spanish diplomat's stolen letter called him 'weak'; then the Maine exploded in Havana harbor.

images.title: The de Lome letter of 1898
images.description: The stolen letter calling McKinley 'weak': the spark before the spark.

images.title: The battleship Maine in Havana harbor
images.description: February 15, 1898: the Maine exploded in Havana harbor, and the yellow press blamed Spain with no evidence.

images.title: The wreck of the Maine in Havana harbor
images.description: Nobody's fully sure what sank the Maine; the likely cause was a boiler failure. Don't write 'Spain sank the Maine' as fact.

images.title: A 'Remember the Maine' poster from 1898
images.description: The slogan wrote itself; America believed Spain guilty, and belief was enough.

images.title: The Teller Amendment of 1898
images.description: Into the April war resolution went the Teller Amendment: no intention of annexing Cuba. Teller is the promise.

images.title: American troops in 1898
images.description: Two down: the outward turn, and the road to war. Now the war itself.

images.title: Theodore Roosevelt in 1898
images.description: Roosevelt, assistant secretary of the navy, cabled Dewey on February 25: be ready to hit the Spanish in the Philippines.

images.title: Portrait of Commodore George Dewey
images.description: When war came, Dewey was ready: on May 1 he sailed into Manila Bay and destroyed the Spanish fleet in a morning.

images.title: A map of the Battle of Manila Bay
images.description: Cuba was the cause; the Philippines were the surprise. If a question asks what started the war, name Cuba and the Maine.

images.title: A map of the Spanish-American War
images.description: The war was fought over Cuba; the empire was the aftershock.

images.title: The Rough Riders at San Juan Hill
images.description: July 1: the heights outside Santiago, Roosevelt's Rough Riders up San Juan Hill; July 3, the Spanish fleet annihilated.

images.title: Portrait of John Hay
images.description: John Hay, the American ambassador in London: 'It has been a splendid little war.'

images.title: American soldiers in Cuba in 1898
images.description: Fewer than four hundred Americans died in combat; about two thousand five hundred total, most to disease.

images.title: The signing of the Treaty of Paris, 1898
images.description: Spain lets go of Cuba; America takes the Philippines, Guam, Puerto Rico. Twenty million dollars, and nobody asked the Filipinos.

images.title: The White House in 1898
images.description: The prediction beat: McKinley, winter of 1898, the treaty's on his desk; sign it, or walk away?

images.title: A map of the Philippines in 1898
images.description: He signed: the Filipinos were 'unfit for self-government,' and the Senate ratified by a single vote.

images.title: Portrait of Emilio Aguinaldo
images.description: Arguing the Filipino case, from 1899: Aguinaldo, who declared Philippine independence on June 12, 1898.

images.title: American goods for export in the 1890s
images.description: The expansionist ledger: the panic proved America needed markets; Mahan proved a great power needs bases.

images.title: Filipino soldiers in 1898
images.description: 'Your ledger skips us': they fought Spain for two years before Dewey's ships arrived and stood beside him at Manila.

images.title: Manila in 1898
images.description: Abandonment meant civil war and a German or Japanese flag over Manila, said the expansionist case.

images.title: Portrait of Mark Twain
images.description: The Anti-Imperialist League: Mark Twain, Andrew Carnegie, William Jennings Bryan. The Revolution in reverse.

images.title: The Philippine-American War, 1899
images.description: Round two: the treaty bought a war, 1899 to 1902, and that's the real imperialism story.

images.title: Filipino troops in 1899
images.description: February 1899: the shooting started between Aguinaldo's soldiers and the Americans, and it hasn't stopped.

images.title: American soldiers in the Philippines in 1899
images.description: The army used the skills it learned fighting Native Americans: three years, more than four thousand American dead.

images.title: An American column in the Philippines
images.description: Honesty first: as many as two hundred thousand Filipino dead in the three-year war.

images.title: An American-run school in the Philippines
images.description: The defense: schools built and local self-government set up, town by town; the threat was real.

images.title: Cuba's constitution of 1901
images.description: Congress swore off annexing Cuba, then wrote the Platt Amendment into Cuba's constitution in 1901.

images.title: Filipino schoolchildren in the 1900s
images.description: 'Schools don't vote': a government that must be taught to want you is a government that doesn't want you.

images.title: Bryan campaigning in 1900
images.description: Bryan ran for president in 1900 on stopping all of this, and lost; the voters chose the empire.

images.title: A cartoon on American imperialism
images.description: Closing statements: rebut, don't repeat. The charge is betrayal, and on Cuba the record convicts.

images.title: The Cuban flag raised in 1902
images.description: Teller promised no annexation; Platt wrote America's right of return into Cuba's constitution.

images.title: The Treaty of Paris document, 1898
images.description: Twenty million dollars. For people. The record says twenty million.

images.title: A Manila street in 1900
images.description: Washington ran what it bought as an uplift project: classrooms built and town councils set up.

images.title: The Philippine flag of 1898
images.description: We declared our independence in 1898; we'd already taken what Spain sold you.

images.title: The Supreme Court in 1901
images.description: In 1901 the Court agreed the Constitution didn't have to follow the flag: necessity or hypocrisy, that's the essay.

images.title: The battleship Oregon in 1898
images.description: Recap one: the 1893 panic and the hunt for markets, Mahan's sea power, the missionaries, Beveridge's new frontier.

images.title: A painting of the Battle of Manila Bay
images.description: Recap three: Dewey at Manila Bay, May 1; San Juan Hill, July 1; Hay's 'splendid little war.'

images.title: Guantanamo Bay in the early 1900s
images.description: Teller's the promise, Platt's the leash: no treaties without American approval, and the Guantanamo base.

images.title: A map of American overseas territories around 1900
images.description: 1898 made America a colonial power: the Philippines, Guam, Puerto Rico, bought and kept.

images.title: Newsboys with the yellow press in 1898
images.description: Read the stimulus for what it did: it made war politically unavoidable, and the SAQ writes itself.

images.title: The text of the Teller Amendment
images.description: Question two: 1898, the Teller Amendment in the war resolution; 1901, the Platt Amendment in Cuba's constitution.

images.title: The Platt Amendment document
images.description: The promise, then the loophole: no annexation, then intervention 'when necessary.'

images.title: American soldiers of the Spanish-American War
images.description: Question three: fewer than four hundred American combat deaths in the summer war.

images.title: Mahan in naval uniform
images.description: Fast bonus: sea power makes great powers; a great navy needs coaling stations and markets worth protecting.

images.title: A naval coaling station in the 1890s
images.description: The book that turned battleships into destiny: stations and markets to protect.

images.title: The American flag in the Philippines
images.description: Four months of war, three years of fighting, and an argument about empire that's still going.
